newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR urges West to protect Zaire refugee routes.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR urges West to protect Zaire refugee routes.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency chief called on Monday for international efforts to create protected humanitarian corridors in Zaire to coax Rwandan refugees back into their homeland.
Sadako Ogata appealed urgently for a ceasefire in eastern Zaire where Tutsi rebels have offered a three-week truce.

"There is now a sense of urgency. With the recent fighting, I'm desperate. I think the only way we can do this is to link up with a lot of governments and U.N. headquarters," Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said in an interview.
"It's a multi-dimensional operation we have to do."

Coincidentally, Tutsi rebels in the Zaire town of Bukavu offered a temporary ceasefire after military successes which have turned more than a million Rwandan Hutus into refugees with little food or water.
At the same time, France proposed an international relief operation and Germany called for a special Security Council meeting on Zaire.
Ogata acknowledged the difficulty of creating safe routes to lure the refugees home when they are heading deeper into Zaire, but said this was a priority to stop the conflict spreading.

"It's a question of how we set it (return corridors) up quickly, especially when the refugees are fleeing to the other direction, westward, under the attack of various fighting forces," the former Japanese academic said.
"The first thing is to stop attacks on refugees or camps. I'm appealing to anybody who is in a position to do that."

Ogata said her UNHCR agency had no access to half a million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees in Uvira and Bukavu regions of east Zaire. Farther north, half a million Rwandan Hutus are packed into the overcrowded Mugunga camp near Goma town, next to Rwanda's northwestern border with Zaire.
The refugees in east Zaire, home to a million Rwandan Hutus who fled in fear of revenge for 1994's Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis, are fleeing fighting between Zairean troops and ethnic Tutsi fighters.
They are afraid to go to Rwanda where a Tutsi-dominated army holds sway. Their camps on Rwanda's borders were staging posts for Hutu militia raids into Rwanda.
Diplomats say the Tutsi rebels, apparently with support from Rwandan forces, are trying to push the Hutus as far away from Rwanda's borders as possible.

The U.N. Security Council on Friday issued a statement calling for a ceasefire but it is unclear how this could be done. Major Western powers and African nations are not keen on international intervention.

The Rwandan refugees in Zaire were costing the international community $1 million a day in aid. Many Western donors will see the latest crisis as the beginning of an end game and are unlikely to be prepared to pay for the creation of new camps.

Ogata, asked if UNHCR would help the Hutus deeper in Zaire, said: "That's is a very difficult question. If they move west, they will be scattered. There may be insecurity spreading all over the region."

If refugees poured into the Masisi region north of Goma, where native Zairean tribes backed by Hutus uprooted thousands of Tutsis earlier this year, Ogata said aid workers would have to meet them from the western part of the territory.
But she said the priority should be establishing a humanitarian corridor from Goma town into Rwanda.
"I'd like to make all our efforts to stop the spread to the west because that would further destabilise Zaire," she said.

"I'd like to have heavy international presence in order to give a sense of confidence to refugees who are very frightened. Trying to convince them requires enormous efforts. I will need both Zairean and Rwandan authorities to make this happen."
